chunk_findings.detail: The fixture creates a real git commit without pinning the commit dates (`GIT_AUTHOR_DATE` / `GIT_COMMITTER_DATE` are absent from the environment fixture, which only scrubs `DDFLOW_*`, `FORCE_COLOR`, `NO_COLOR` and sets `COLUMNS`). `git commit` fills author/committer date with the current wall-clock (and the local timezone offset), and both are part of the object that is hashed. So the SHA of `HEAD` — and therefore of every derived short/long hash — is different on every run and on every machine. The fixture exists precisely because ddflow surfaces git provenance (the whole point of `git init`/`config`/`commit` here is to give the brief/recall/exports a stable repo), so any golden that prints the HEAD sha (e.g. the brief header, or an export that records `git rev-parse HEAD`) is non-deterministic: run `uv run pytest tests/golden` twice, or run it on a machine in a different timezone, and the snapshot diffs even though no code changed. The fix is to export fixed `GIT_AUTHOR_DATE`/`GIT_COMMITTER_DATE` (and clear any inherited `GIT_*`) around the commit.
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/conftest.py `project` fixture (the `git commit -qm "init"` call)

chunk_findings.detail: `re.sub(rf"(?<![\w.]){re.escape(__version__)}(?![\w.])", ...)` will not replace the version whenever the character immediately before it is a word character. Given the common CLI spelling `ddflow v0.1.0`, the preceding char is `v` (a `\w`), so the negative lookbehind fails, no substitution happens, and the raw version string is baked into the golden. The same is true for a build-string form such as `0.1.0.dev0`, where the trailing `.` in the lookahead `(?![\w.])` also blocks the match. In those cases the normaliser silently does nothing and the golden breaks on the next version bump — the exact failure it is supposed to prevent — rather than being version-independent. (Conditional on the CLI printing the version adjacent to a word char/dot; a plain `ddflow 0.1.0` does match.)
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/conftest.py `normalise` version regex

chunk_findings.detail: The `id` on the `research.recorded` line is `e74721cbed98fa006bd15157d`, which is 25 hex characters, while every other id in this fixture (and the writer's generated ids, which are 24-hex) is exactly 24. The whole point of the fixture is to exercise real writer payload shapes, so this is an invalid shape. Concretely: if the event loader validates id width/format when reading the JSONL, loading this fixture raises and every golden/property test built on it fails with a load error rather than exercising behaviour; if the loader happens not to validate, the property tests then pin behaviour for an id no real writer can emit, i.e. the "properties hold for real writer payload shapes" guarantee is lost for this record. Either way the snapshot/golden suite is testing an unreachable input. Fixing it to a 24-hex id (and regenerating any snapshot whose subject/subject-derived value comes from this id, e.g. `R49b608db82`) is needed.
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/fixtures/project.jsonl:9 (event `R49b608db82` / `research.recorded`)

chunk_findings.detail: `unwrap_usage` normalises only the first paragraph (`text.partition("\n\n")`). But argparse computes its layout width from the *environment*, not from the snapshot: `HelpFormatter.__init__` does `width = shutil.get_terminal_size().columns - 2`, and `shutil.get_terminal_size()` returns `int(os.environ["COLUMNS"])` when that variable is set, otherwise the size of `sys.__stdout__.fileno()` (which succeeds when capture is disabled, e.g. `pytest -s` on a real terminal) and only falls back to 80 when both are unavailable. The description and the `options:`/`positional arguments:` sections are filled/wrapped at that width (`_fill_text`, `_format_action`), and none of that is normalised by `unwrap_usage`, which only touches the `usage` paragraph. Concrete repro: `COLUMNS=40 pytest tests/golden/test_golden_cli_help.py::test_help` (or running the file with `-s` in a terminal wider/narrower than 80 columns) produces `format_help()` whose description/option help wraps at different points than the .ambr recorded at width 78, so the assertion fails although the CLI interface is unchanged. This contradicts the stated goal that the goldens be deterministic across machines. Passing an explicit width to the parser/formatter (or whitespace-normalising every paragraph, not just the first) is needed to make this golden environment-independent.
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/test_golden_cli_help.py:52 (`unwrap_usage` / `test_help`)

chunk_findings.detail: The guard filters candidate document names with `r.islower() and r.isalpha()`, so its set of "documents" is restricted to strings in `[a-z]+`. That defeats the stated purpose ("A new export document must be added to EXPORTS, or it ships unpinned") for any name that is not pure lowercase ASCII letters: a name containing a digit, hyphen, or underscore is dropped from `rows` by the filter before comparison. Concretely, if the CLI later adds an export document `release-notes` (or `v2worklog`), and the maintainer correctly adds `"release-notes"` to `EXPORTS`, `rows` never contains it, so `rows == EXPORTS` fails even though the listing is correct — a false failure. In the other direction, if the maintainer forgets to add `release-notes` to `EXPORTS`, the filter also drops it from `rows`, so the check passes vacuously and the new document ships unpinned. The same filter also silently discards any unindented lowercase-alpha footer/usage token (e.g. a line beginning `run ...`), which would turn into a spurious row and a false failure if such a line is ever emitted. The check should compare the listing's document column structurally rather than by an ad-hoc alphabetic heuristic.
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/test_golden_outputs.py:35 (`test_the_export_list_names_every_document_pinned_here`)

chunk_findings.detail: The docstring of `event_logs` states the returned list is "A merged log in the order `read_all` returns it: ... sorted by (lamport, agent, id) **and de-duplicated**", but the body only does `return sorted(out, key=Event.sort_key)` — no de-duplication step exists. Because the whole premise of the generator (spelled out in the same docstring) is that "clones that did not see each other can reuse a value", two independently generated events can coincide on the fields that determine an event's identity (`kind`, `subject`, `data`, and the reused Lamport value), i.e. they are the same event id; `read_all` collapses such a pair to a single event, whereas this strategy emits both. Any property that is supposed to pin read_all semantics (e.g. "replay equals live", or a fold whose result depends on the number/ordering of events) is therefore exercised on a log that `read_all` can never return, so it can fail — or pass vacuously because the duplicate is folded as if it were two distinct events — for reasons that do not exist in production. The fix is to merge on the event id (e.g. keep the first/last per id before/after sorting) so the fixture actually matches the documented `read_all` output.
chunk_findings.title: tests/property/evstrategies.py:146 (`event_logs`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The assertion compares a deduplicated input on the left with the raw generated log on the right:

```python
assert _sorted_unique(shuffled) == _sorted_unique(events)          # ok
assert fold(_sorted_unique(shuffled), strict=False) == fold(events, strict=False)
```

The left operand is the normalized union (`_sorted_unique` collapses repeated events); the right operand is the un-normalized `events`. The module's stated property is only that "however the shards are concatenated, the *sorted union* folds the same" (and the sibling test `test_a_duplicated_history_folds_like_the_history_once` deliberately deduplicates **both** sides with `_sorted_unique` before folding, i.e. it treats a repeated event as fold-visible and therefore not safe to fold twice). So if the generated log ever contains the same event twice (which is exactly the situation the duplication test constructs), the two sides fold different histories: the left applies that event once, the right applies it twice, the resulting `State`s differ, and the assertion fails even though the fold is order-free as documented. The right-hand side should be `fold(_sorted_unique(events), strict=False)`; as written it pins an undocumented "fold also normalizes duplicates" property that the rest of the file does not assume.
chunk_findings.title: tests/property/test_fold_properties.py:70 (`test_the_order_shards_are_read_in_does_not_matter`)

chunk_findings.detail: The property is stated as "no two ready items' globs overlap (a shared glob overlaps nothing)", but both assertions (`not conflicts(a.globs, b.globs, shared)` and `not conflicts(it.globs, lease.globs, shared)`) call the *same* `conflicts` predicate that `schedule.plan` uses internally to decide what is offerable. This makes the check tautological with respect to `conflicts` itself: it can only detect plan failing to call `conflicts`, never a bug inside `conflicts`. Concrete vacuous pass: if a refactor makes `conflicts` return `False` for two identical non-shared globs (e.g. `conflicts(["src/a.py"], ["src/a.py"], []) == False`, e.g. by an over-eager "a shared glob overlaps nothing" carve‑out or an equality/short-circuit change), then plan will emit two ready items that genuinely both write `src/a.py`, and the assertion still passes because `conflicts` also says they don't conflict. The deps property avoids exactly this by writing its own `_deps_met`; this property does not, so the class of regression it exists to pin ("no conflicting offers") can slip through.
chunk_findings.title: tests/property/test_scheduler_properties.py:97 (`test_no_two_offers_conflict_and_none_overlaps_another_agents_lease`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The second half of the same test takes "another agent's live lease" from `state.active_leases`, which is the production helper `plan` itself relies on for lease awareness. If `active_leases` regresses (e.g. stops returning a lease whose `taken`/`heartbeat` is within `grace_s`, or mis-handles the `shared_globs` argument), the test will simply not see the lease and will pass while plan hands out an offer that collides with a live lease. A hand-rolled oracle (e.g. scanning raw lease events against `now - grace_s`) would be needed to make this check able to fail.

---

Everything else in the file (offset lamports on the tail, `fold(..., strict=False)`, `max_examples=150`/`database=None`, the free-slot bound, the bucket-partition and determinism assertions) I could not break with the generated shapes.
chunk_findings.title: tests/property/test_scheduler_properties.py:103 (lease-liveness oracle)

chunk_findings.detail: The fixture's whole stated purpose is "Nothing from the developer's shell reaches the output: no `DDFLOW_*` override (each would show as an `[env]` source)", and the loop clears every `DDFLOW_*` variable — except `DDFLOW_LAUNCH_ROOT`, which is explicitly exempted and neither cleared nor re-pinned to the temporary repo. That leaves the golden output dependent on the ambient shell, in two concrete ways. (a) If `main` reports its configuration sources (the `[env]` lines the comment is worried about), a developer who has the ddflow shell integration active, e.g. `export DDFLOW_LAUNCH_ROOT=/home/dev/realproj`, gets an extra/changed `[env] DDFLOW_LAUNCH_ROOT=...` line in `tools/list`/`brief`/`recall` output that was not present when the snapshot was recorded (CI usually has the variable unset), so the "byte-identical across machines" property fails without any code change. (b) If the CLI uses `DDFLOW_LAUNCH_ROOT` for repo/launch-root resolution, then `main(["--repo", str(project), "--agent", "golden", *argv])` is run with a value pointing at the developer's real repository rather than `tmp_path/proj`, so the captured output is produced from the wrong project — and any mutating golden test would write into that real repo instead of the fixture. Demonstration: `DDFLOW_LAUNCH_ROOT=$HOME/myproject uv run pytest tests/golden` versus a clean `env -u DDFLOW_LAUNCH_ROOT uv run pytest tests/golden`; the two runs must not be able to differ, but with the exemption in place they can. Either delete it like every other `DDFLOW_*` key, or set it explicitly to `str(project)` so it is a pinned input rather than an inherited one.
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/conftest.py:33-36 (`_pinned_environment` / `DDFLOW_LAUNCH_ROOT`)

chunk_findings.detail: `format_help()` is produced by `argparse.HelpFormatter`, and when `build_parser()` does not pass an explicit `width`, the formatter derives its width from `shutil.get_terminal_size()` (i.e. the `COLUMNS` env var, else the size of fd 1, else the 80x24 fallback). `unwrap_usage` only normalises the leading `usage:` paragraph; everything after the first `\n\n` (the description and the options/arguments sections) is snapshotted raw, and those sections wrap at `self._width` (`_format_text` uses `text_width = self._width - indent`, `_format_action` derives `help_position`/`help_width` from `self._width`). So the snapshot only matches when the effective width happens to be the one used to record the `.ambr`. Concrete failure: under pytest's default fd capture the fallback is 80, but `COLUMNS=140 pytest tests/golden/test_golden_cli_help.py` (or `pytest -s` / `--capture=no` run from a 140-column terminal, which is the common way to debug) makes fd 1 a tty of width 140, `format_help()` wraps any long description or long option help at 138 columns instead of 78, and the assert fails although nothing in `ddflow/` changed. This contradicts the stated goal that the goldens are deterministic across machines; the recording and the assertion environments differ in a variable the test never pins.
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/test_golden_cli_help.py: unwrap_usage / test_help

chunk_findings.detail: The guard is claimed by its own docstring to fail "or it ships unpinned" whenever a new export document appears, but the filter `[r for r in rows if r.islower() and r.isalpha()]` silently discards any row whose name is not purely lowercase alphabetic. `"release-notes".islower()` is True but `"release-notes".isalpha()` is False; `"audit2".isalpha()` is False; and any name containing `_`, `.`, or a digit is dropped the same way. So if a future export is registered as `release-notes` (or `by-file`, `audit2`, ...), the listing gains that row, the filter removes it, and the assertion still compares `[...] == EXPORTS` and passes — exactly the "ships unpinned" case the test exists to prevent. The test only catches new exports whose names happen to be pure lowercase ASCII letters. A stronger form would compare the parsed row names without the `islower`/`isalpha` narrowing (or assert that every parsed name is in `EXPORTS` and that the sets are equal) so non-alphabetic names cannot slip through.
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/test_golden_outputs.py:38-41 (`test_the_export_list_names_every_document_pinned_here`)

chunk_findings.detail: `event_logs` documents itself as returning "A merged log in the order `read_all` returns it: ... sorted by (lamport, agent, id) and de-duplicated," but the function only sorts — it never de-duplicates, and it is *constructed* so that de-duplication can never matter: within one agent, `clocks[agent] = floor + draw(st.integers(1, 3))` is strictly increasing across every draw, so no two events can share `(agent, lamport)`, and each `(kind, subject, data)` is drawn exactly once. Therefore no two generated events can share an `id` (any `compute_id` that includes the agent and/or the lamport, as it must for `read_all` to be able to dedup a merged log at all, already makes them distinct here). Consequently the claimed "de-duplicated" property is never exercised: a property test of the form "fold(merged log) == fold(deduped merged log)" or "re-ingesting an already-seen event is idempotent" (the scenario where the same event ends up in two shards and `read_all` collapses it) passes vacuously on every input this strategy can produce. Two concrete notes: (1) the stated emulation of `read_all` is false — the generator cannot emit a log that needs the very de-duplication it advertises; (2) if `Event.compute_id()` is content-addressed without the agent in the hash, the missing de-duplication is worse than a no-op, because two different agents producing the same `(kind, subject, data)` at the same Lamport value would then emit two events with identical ids into a log that `read_all` would never return, and a fold comparing "live" to "replayed" would diverge. Either way, the de-duplication step the docstring promises is absent from the code.
chunk_findings.title: tests/property/evstrategies.py:event_logs (return statement, `return sorted(out, key=Event.sort_key)`)

chunk_findings.detail: The test never folds a duplicated log. `once` is `fold(_sorted_unique(events))` and the comparison is `fold(_sorted_unique(twice)) == once`, but `_sorted_unique` is exactly the sort-and-dedup union, so when it works (which is the assumption the property rests on) `_sorted_unique(twice)` is the identical list to `_sorted_unique(events)`, and the assertion collapses to `fold(Y) == fold(Y)` for Y = `_sorted_unique(events)`. Consequently the asserted property ("a log read with every event twice folds to the same State as the log read once") is not exercised: the duplicates are removed by `_sorted_unique` before `fold` ever sees them. Concretely, if `fold` were changed so that a log containing an event twice double-counts it (breaking fold-level idempotence), the test would still pass, because it only ever calls `fold` on a de-duplicated list. A test that pinned the claim would fold `twice` (the raw concatenation) and compare that to `once`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/property/test_fold_properties.py:62 (test_a_duplicated_history_folds_like_the_history_once)

chunk_findings.detail: The test cannot detect order-dependence in `fold`, which is what it is named for. `shuffled` is a permutation of `events`, so `_sorted_unique(shuffled) == _sorted_unique(events)` at line 70 is true by construction of sort+dedup and contributes nothing; and at line 71 the shuffled list is re-canonicalized by `_sorted_unique` before `fold` sees it, then compared against `fold(events)` where `event_logs()` emits a log (i.e. already in canonical order). Both sides therefore fold the same canonical list, so the assertion is `fold(X) == fold(X)`. Concretely, if `fold` were changed to aggregate strictly in the order events arrive, this test still passes because no shuffled list is ever handed to `fold`; to pin order-freeness the shuffle would have to be folded directly (`fold(shuffled) == fold(events)`), not through `_sorted_unique`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/property/test_fold_properties.py:70-71 (test_the_order_shards_are_read_in_does_not_matter)

chunk_findings.detail:
The oracle's skip rule does not implement the behaviour its own docstring describes. The docstring says an ancestor's need is exempt when it is "an umbrella's need on its own child ... met by running it -- `inherited_deps`", but the code only exempts a need whose target is inside the *offered item's* subtree (`own_subtree = descendants(item_id) | {item_id}`), so a need on an ancestor of the offered item is never exempted.

Concrete input (all events valid `task.added`s; `event_logs`/`task.added` supports arbitrary `parent`+`needs`, and the composite draws both):
- `A` parent `""`, `needs: ["C"]`
- `C` parent `"A"`, `needs: []`
- `D` parent `"C"`, `needs: []`

`plan` must offer `D` once nothing else blocks it: `inherited_deps(D)` cannot contain `C`, otherwise `C` (an umbrella, never offered itself) could only become DONE after `D` and its siblings run, while `D` waits for `C` to be DONE — a deadlock, so the scheduler necessarily exempts an ancestor's need on one of its own children/ancestors of the item. But `_deps_met(state, "D")` walks `D -> C -> A`, and at `cur = A` it sees `dep = "C"`; because `C` is an ancestor of `D`, `C not in own_subtree("D")`, so it falls through to `d.state != DONE` and returns `False`. `test_an_offer_is_never_made_before_its_dependencies` then asserts `_deps_met(state, it.id)` and fails even though the offer is legitimate — a false failure. The exemption should be based on the ancestor/path relation (a need pointing at a node whose subtree contains the offered item), not solely on the item's own descendants.
chunk_findings.title: tests/property/test_scheduler_properties.py: `_deps_met` (lines ~69–86)

data.summary: inherited_deps hands a grandchild its ancestor's need on the grandchild's own parent: A needs C, C is A's child, D is C's child -> D blocked 'C is open (inherited from A)' while C is an umbrella waiting on D: a permanent hang (the subtree exemption covers only the item's own descendants, not its ancestors between it and the need's owner)
data.title: Umbrella need on its own child deadlocks that child's sub-tasks

data.body:
Fixes bug B43447abfc8: inherited_deps hands a grandchild its ancestor's need on the grandchild's own parent: A needs C, C is A's child, D is C's child -> D blocked 'C is open (inherited from A)' while C is an umbrella waiting on D: a permanent hang (the subtree exemption covers only the item's own descendants, not its ancestors between it and the need's owner)

Write the regression test first and watch it FAIL on the unfixed code; then `ddflow complete fix-B43447abfc8 --regression-test <test>` closes the bug with the task (or `ddflow bug fixed B43447abfc8 --regression-test <test>` first).
